idiom_name: one struct: embedded base for the first protocol, interfaces for the second (promotion replaces the twin link)
implementation_notes: Go has no inheritance: embedding promotes the embedded type's fields and methods - the spec says promoted fields 'act like ordinary fields of a struct' and the promoted methods join the outer type's method set - and interface satisfaction is implicit, so a single struct can be both 'a base' and 'an implementer of a second protocol' without a second object. What replaces the twin's crossing calls: explicit forwarding methods on the outer struct, because the embedded type's methods receive the embedded value as receiver and have no idea they were embedded - promotion is compile-time sugar with no dynamic dispatch. Keep the classic pair of objects only when two independent subsystems must each hold their own concrete value (two maps keyed by different concrete types) or when mutual re-entrancy needs two addressable objects; Go's collector handles cycles, so mutual pointers are safe here, unlike in reference-counted languages.
pitfalls: A promoted method's receiver is the embedded value, not the outer struct: it cannot see the outer struct's fields, so overriding behaviour requires a written forwarding method - the point where a naive port of the twin's forwarding half goes wrong.
Embedding a pointer type shares the embedded value and promotes pointer-receiver methods, while embedding by value copies it: mutating promoted state can then silently mutate a copy.
Promotion resolves at compile time with no virtual dispatch - a promoted method that calls another method of the embedded type calls the embedded type's version, never the outer struct's override.
Embedding an interface in a struct that never receives a concrete value compiles fine and panics on the first promoted call (nil interface).
